name: King-Denborough syndrome (RYR1, malignant hyperthermia-associated)
aliases: malignant hyperthermia with dysmorphism and myopathy

reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: A rare congenital myopathy caused predominantly by RYR1 variants, combining slowly progressive muscle weakness, characteristic dysmorphic features, and malignant hyperthermia susceptibility
Dysmorphic features classically include short stature, a myopathic facies, low-set ears, downslanting palpebral fissures, ptosis, high-arched palate, webbed neck, pectus deformity, and scoliosis
Presents in childhood with hypotonia, proximal weakness, and delayed motor milestones, and progression is usually slow
Malignant hyperthermia susceptibility is the defining safety concern, so exposure to triggering anaesthetic agents must be avoided

Volatile inhalational anaesthetics and depolarising neuromuscular blockers (suxamethonium) are the principal malignant hyperthermia triggers to avoid, and dantrolene must be immediately available where anaesthesia is undertaken
Creatine kinase is often mildly to moderately elevated and electromyography shows a myopathic pattern
Muscle biopsy findings are variable and may show non-specific myopathic changes, cores, or fibre-type disproportion, so genetics are important for confirmation
Diagnosis integrates the myopathy, the recognisable dysmorphic phenotype, and RYR1 genetic testing, with formal malignant hyperthermia (in-vitro contracture) testing where available
reference.pathophysiology: King-Denborough syndrome is most often caused by variants in RYR1, the gene encoding the skeletal muscle ryanodine receptor, the calcium-release channel of the sarcoplasmic reticulum that is central to excitation-contraction coupling. Abnormal channel function disturbs regulated calcium release, impairing muscle contraction and producing a congenital myopathy, while the same channel abnormality renders muscle liable to uncontrolled calcium release and hypermetabolic crisis on exposure to triggering anaesthetic agents, the basis of malignant hyperthermia susceptibility. The associated dysmorphic and skeletal features form part of the recognisable syndromic phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Other RYR1-related congenital myopathies (central core disease, multiminicore disease)
Noonan syndrome and other dysmorphic syndromes with short stature and webbed neck
Isolated malignant hyperthermia susceptibility without overt myopathy
additionalInvestigations: Muscle biopsy with histochemistry, which may show cores or fibre-type disproportion
Genetic testing of RYR1 and a congenital myopathy panel
Referral for malignant hyperthermia evaluation, including in-vitro/caffeine-halothane contracture testing where available
Cardiac and respiratory assessment and monitoring of scoliosis
redFlags: Any planned anaesthesia, given the high risk of triggering a malignant hyperthermia crisis
Personal or family history of an unexplained anaesthetic reaction, rigidity, or hyperthermia
Respiratory muscle weakness or progressive scoliosis compromising ventilation
Episodes of rhabdomyolysis or exertional hyperthermia
reference.prognosis: The myopathy itself is usually slowly progressive and compatible with prolonged ambulation and a reasonable lifespan, but the malignant hyperthermia susceptibility poses a serious perioperative risk; with recognition, trigger avoidance, and availability of dantrolene, life-threatening anaesthetic crises are largely preventable.
pitfalls: Failing to recognise malignant hyperthermia susceptibility before surgery and using triggering agents
Not ensuring dantrolene and a trigger-free anaesthetic technique are available for affected patients
Attributing the dysmorphic features to another syndrome and missing the underlying RYR1 myopathy
Assuming a normal or non-specific muscle biopsy excludes the diagnosis without genetic testing
Omitting family screening and anaesthetic counselling for at-risk relatives

management: Strict avoidance of malignant hyperthermia triggers, namely volatile inhalational anaesthetics and the depolarising neuromuscular blocker suxamethonium, using trigger-free total intravenous anaesthesia instead
Ensure dantrolene is immediately available wherever anaesthesia is undertaken
Malignant hyperthermia crisis protocol with intravenous dantrolene, active cooling and correction of hyperkalaemia and acidosis
Physiotherapy and rehabilitation to maintain strength and ambulation in the congenital myopathy
Respiratory monitoring, cardiac assessment and orthopaedic management of scoliosis
Documented malignant hyperthermia alert and medical-alert identification, with evaluation and counselling of at-risk family members
Referral for malignant hyperthermia contracture testing and RYR1 genetic testing
